#6337. Why do some autumn leaves change color early? Weather alone can’t explain it

A new study suggests the balance of nutrients inside leaves helps explain why some forests lose their summer green earlier than others.

Shorter days, cooler temperatures, and rainfall all help determine when autumn leaves turn. But weather doesn’t explain all of it, and a new study suggests part of the answer is inside the leaves themselves.

In most of the forests the researchers studied, from Alaska to Hawaii, leaves that held a lot of nitrogen compared with phosphorus lost their summer green earlier in the fall.

A leaf’s chemistry, in other words, seems to carry clues about autumn timing that the weather alone misses.

The study was led by Tong Qiu, an assistant professor of ecology at Duke University’s Nicholas School of the Environment, with Ph.D. candidate Hanshi Chen as first author.

The team worked entirely from airplane and satellite measurements, so the results show a consistent pattern, not proof that nutrients cause the change.

Leaves need nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium to do their job.

These nutrients help build proteins and chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves, and they help a leaf make and use sugar.

Together, these processes help leaves keep producing food late into the growing season.

The balance between these nutrients has been changing. For decades, farms and industry have released extra nitrogen into the environment.

A 2013 analysis by Josep Peñuelas and colleagues linked human-caused imbalances between nitrogen and phosphorus to changes in natural and farmed ecosystems worldwide.

Peñuelas is also an author of the new study, which notes that rising nitrogen levels are leaving many ecosystems relatively short on phosphorus. What that means for autumn hasn’t been clear.

Checking leaf nutrients across a whole continent is also slow and expensive.

“Usually, measuring nutrients requires people to collect leaves and go back to the lab and do an experiment to quantify their concentrations,” Qiu said.

Instead of collecting leaves, the team used data from the National Ecological Observatory Network, a group of U.S. research sites funded by the National Science Foundation.

A plane flies over each site carrying an imaging spectrometer. This kind of camera records sunlight bouncing off the trees in 426 narrow bands, most of them invisible to the human eye.

Leaves with different amounts of nutrients reflect light a little differently.

Scientists had already matched these readings to about 300 leaf samples from sunlit treetops, and the method was most accurate for nitrogen.

Qiu’s team used this approach to map nutrients across 25 forest sites.

They ranged from Alaska and the mountains of the West to a Texas woodland and a wet mountain forest on volcanic soil in Hawaii.

To track autumn, the team used satellite images sharp enough to show areas about 10 feet (3 meters) across.

For each spot, they identified the fall day when greenness fell near its seasonal minimum, reaching the bottom 15% of its annual range.

The researchers then compared spots within the same forest. They divided each forest site into squares about 100 feet (30 meters) wide, analyzing roughly 4,600 to 62,000 squares per site.

In 20 of the 25 forests, spots where leaves held more nitrogen relative to phosphorus lost their green earlier.

That held even after the team accounted for weather, elevation, tree species, and canopy height.

“There seems to be a sweet spot where nitrogen and phosphorus are in balance,” Qiu said. “If that gets crossed, trees will start changing color earlier.”

The likely reason, the authors wrote, has to do with phosphorus, which cells need to carry energy.

When phosphorus runs low, energy transfer within cells could slow, potentially causing leaves to lose their green earlier.

As leaves shut down for the season, trees break down their chlorophyll and move phosphorus out of the leaves into parts that live through the winter.

Not every forest followed this pattern. In two mountain evergreen forests in the West and at the Hawaiian site, leaves with more nitrogen relative to phosphorus stayed green longer.

In places like these, the authors suggested, extra nitrogen may ease a nitrogen shortage instead of signaling a lack of phosphorus.

With potassium, the pattern flipped. In 19 of the 25 forests, leaves with more nitrogen relative to potassium stayed green longer.

Potassium helps a leaf open and close the tiny pores that let in carbon dioxide, and it helps send sugar to the rest of the tree.

The researchers proposed that when a tree has plenty of potassium, extra nitrogen may help its leaves keep their chlorophyll and keep making food longer.

Two eastern forests, where potassium seemed to be in short supply, showed the reverse. There, leaves with more nitrogen relative to potassium lost their green sooner.

Weather still played a role. In 15 of the 25 forests, spots that got more rain during the growing season tended to stay green longer.

When the team added nutrient information to a model based on weather alone, the model did a better job explaining autumn timing in 22 of the 25 forests.

The authors wrote that forecasts of how long forests stay green could improve if they included nutrients.

That matters for more than fall scenery. Leaves that shut down early stop taking in carbon dioxide early, which gives a forest less time each year to store carbon.

Qiu said an imbalance between nitrogen and phosphorus “is bad for vegetation.”

According to Qiu, the findings could also matter for farm businesses such as orchards, since a productive growing season generally goes with later leaf drop.

Nitrogen released by human activity will likely keep rising, he said, so growers “might need to apply phosphorus to balance out the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio.”

Orchards weren’t part of the study, though, which looked only at forests and didn’t test adding phosphorus.

The nutrient maps are estimates based on reflected light, not lab tests of individual trees. The authors describe their explanations as plausible, not proven.

Each forest was also mapped during just one summer, when the trees were at their greenest. So the study compares spots within a forest but can’t yet show what happens to the same trees from year to year.

Continued nitrogen pollution, the authors expect, will leave more forests short on phosphorus, a shift that could be linked to earlier autumns and shorter growing seasons.

To find out, they suggest mapping the same forests again and again, across seasons and years. That would show whether leaves start losing their green earlier as a forest’s nutrient balance changes.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6335. Why are ultra-processed foods linked to heart disease? New clues found in the bloodstream

Blood patterns offer new clues to why ultra-processed foods are linked to heart disease, beyond their sugar, salt and saturated fat content.

Sugar, salt and saturated fat might seem to explain why many ultra-processed foods are linked to heart disease.

But a recent study suggests the connection may involve more than those familiar ingredients.

The research followed British civil servants over many years.

A pattern in their blood offered a stronger clue, accounting for about half the link between ultra-processed food and cardiovascular disease.

The finding raises another possibility: how a food is made may matter alongside what goes into it. For now, that’s a possibility, not a proven cause.

Eunice Wang conducted the research while studying for her PhD at University College London, working with colleagues at UCL and Imperial College London.

“We know there is a link between ultra-processed food and disease, but there is uncertainty over what is driving this connection – whether it is due to higher levels of sugar, salt and saturated fat, as well as dense calorie content, or whether the risks also come from food processing,” Wang said.

The team followed people’s health rather than assigning them different diets. That means the researchers could look for links, but couldn’t show that processing caused anyone’s illness.

“Our findings hint that processing itself may play a role, although more research is needed to support this,” Wang said.

These weren’t people recruited for a new diet experiment. They were 6,010 members of Whitehall II, a study that started in 1985 with civil servants working in London government offices.

By the late 1990s, when they gave the blood samples used here, none had heart disease or diabetes.

They had completed questionnaires covering 127 foods twice during that decade.

Two researchers went through the list and used a system called Nova to decide where each food belonged.

Nova groups foods according to their processing. To qualify as ultra-processed, a product consists mostly of substances taken out of foods and combined with additives. Little or none of the whole food remains.

At the other end are minimally processed foods: fruit and vegetables, whole grains and beans, fish and meat. Water and unsweetened tea and coffee belong there too.

For this study, the team counted food and drink by weight. Calories weren’t the yardstick. That allowed them to include drinks that contain no calories.

On that basis, about 18% of what a typical person consumed each day was ultra-processed. The share for minimally processed food was much larger, at about 62%.

Next came the blood samples. The team examined 233 measures, from sugars and amino acids to fats and the particles that carry them.

From these, they picked out 34 measures closely linked to ultra-processed diets and 50 linked to minimally processed diets.

Together, those measures formed two blood patterns, or “signatures.” Each participant received two scores showing how closely their blood measurements matched each pattern.

One difference concerned omega-3 fats, including DHA. Their levels were lower in the blood of people who ate more ultra-processed food.

HDL particles, the carriers of so-called good cholesterol, were lower too. Particles associated with fatty deposits in arteries were more plentiful.

The pattern looked different among people who ate more minimally processed food. They had more omega-3 and other polyunsaturated fats in their blood. Saturated fat accounted for a smaller proportion.

Of the foods examined, fish stood out for its connection with omega-3.

Ultra-processed meats, sweets and ready-to-eat meals stood out among ultra-processed foods, with the strongest and most consistent links to less healthy blood readings.

The team also had years of health records to work with. Across a typical 20-year follow-up, those records showed 1,094 cases of cardiovascular disease, meaning disease of the heart or blood vessels.

For type 2 diabetes, the typical follow-up was about 18 years. There were 853 cases.

To compare diets, the team put people into thirds according to their ultra-processed food intake.

Those in the highest third had a 23% higher cardiovascular disease risk and an 18% higher diabetes risk than those in the lowest third.

These figures took account of age, smoking, exercise and body weight, as well as sugar, salt, fat and fiber in people’s diets.

The same comparison for minimally processed food went in the other direction.

People in the highest third had an 18% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and a 15% lower risk of diabetes than those in the lowest third.

Blood scores were also linked to later disease. People whose blood most closely matched the minimally processed pattern had a 40% lower risk of type 2 diabetes than those whose blood matched it least.

A closer match to the ultra-processed pattern went with about a 20% higher risk of both diseases.

Accounting for people’s reported diets weakened these connections slightly, but didn’t remove them. Blood measurements may therefore capture details that people miss when describing what they eat.

The team estimated that the ultra-processed blood pattern accounted for 51% of the diet’s link with cardiovascular disease and 43% of its link with diabetes.

For the minimally processed pattern, the figures were 47% and 48%.

Salt and saturated fat explained no detectable part of any link in these calculations.

Sugar didn’t explain either diet’s connection with cardiovascular disease, although it accounted for about 27% of the ultra-processed food link with diabetes.

The blood patterns left roughly half of the associations unexplained.

The authors suggested that gut bacteria, inflammation and changes in appetite or fullness might also play a role.

Processing can alter a food’s physical structure and produce new compounds.

Additives and chemicals that pass from packaging into food might also matter, but the study didn’t establish their roles.

Nor did every ultra-processed food show the same association.

Ultra-processed drinks and meats were linked to higher risks of both diseases, while ultra-processed breads were linked to a lower diabetes risk.

Senior author Clare Llewellyn works in UCL’s department of Behavioural Science and Health.

“Current UK dietary guidance does not consider processing itself as a risk but recommends a reduced intake of foods high in ingredients such as sugar, salt and saturated fat,” Llewellyn said.

Llewellyn said the findings could help discussions about whether dietary guidance should consider processing alongside nutrition.

The Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition, an independent adviser to the UK government, is reviewing the evidence on ultra-processed food and health.

There are gaps in this study, too. People had to remember what they ate, and the questionnaires didn’t cover all the details needed to sort foods by processing.

Nor could the blood tests pick up additives, chemicals from packaging or changes in gut bacteria.

Another catch: the same people supplied the data used to build the blood patterns and to test them. A pattern that looks convincing in that group might be less useful in another.

The calculations used to explain parts of each link also depended on assumptions the study couldn’t check.

Most participants were white male civil servants in midlife, and their food records dated from the 1990s.

Since ultra-processed foods have become more common, the authors suggested their estimates may understate today’s links.

Earlier research has found similar blood patterns. Feeding trials have also found differences in blood and urine between diets with and without ultra-processed foods.

What remains uncertain is why roughly half of these links went unexplained, and whether processing itself causes harm. The authors want the work repeated in more varied groups, using other blood-testing methods.

The study is published in the journal BMC Medicine.

#6334. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

A Roman-era belt buckle discovered in a Ukrainian forest hints at the ancient conflict between the Romans and the Dacians.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Ukraine have found a colorful belt buckle that may have been worn by a nomadic equestrian warrior 1,800 years ago on the fringes of the Roman Empire.

The belt buckle was unearthed by local residents in the Tsetsyn Forest in southeastern Ukraine and given to Antonii Moisei, a professor at Bukovinian State Medical University, according to a translated statement. The roughly square metal buckle, which is about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) on each side, has teal, blue and yellow enamel decorations.

The style of the decoration and the metal construction place the creation of the buckle in the second to third centuries A.D., when this part of Ukraine was in the ancient province of Roman Dacia, according to Moisei.

The column that the Roman emperor Trajan erected in Rome following the empire's triumph in the Dacian Wars.

Under Emperor Trajan, Rome fought the Dacian Wars (A.D. 101-102 and 105-106) against the denizens of the Dacian kingdom and its leader, Decebalus. Roman legions destroyed Dacia and annexed it as a new province. Trajan celebrated his victory in Rome, complete with a famous column that depicts details of the Dacian Wars.

In addition to the buckle, Moisei collected a decorative belt fitting and three small, round metal objects that probably belonged to the same belt. Moisei created a reconstruction of what the belt might have looked like before it was lost in the forest nearly two millennia ago.

But it's unclear who lost the belt. One of Moisei's theories is that the belt belonged to a horse-riding Sarmatian warrior originally from the Black Sea region. The Sarmatians were a group of tribes that lived outside the borders of the Roman Empire, in what are now central Ukraine, southern Russia and the Balkans. While some Sarmatian warriors fought against the incursion of the Roman Empire, others fought with Rome as mercenaries.

The metal belt fragments are part of a Roman provincial craft tradition, according to the statement, and they may have been obtained through trade or as a trophy of war. But Moisei is still studying the artifacts to confirm whether they were Sarmatian. Either way, the military belt provides new evidence of Roman military contact on the outskirts of the empire, and future work could help experts understand how the Romans interacted with the local Dacians during wartime.

#6331. Mount Kilimanjaro reveals a surprising temperature divide as the climate changes

Mount Kilimanjaro’s summit is warming while parts of its middle slopes cool, with expanding vegetation offering a possible explanation.

The summit of Mount Kilimanjaro is warming, while parts of its middle slopes are cooling.

Expanding vegetation may help explain why temperatures are moving in opposite directions on the same mountain.

A temperature analysis spanning almost 5,000 meters of elevation reveals that Africa’s tallest mountain isn’t warming uniformly.

The study was led by PhD student Yaping Mo and professor Nick Pepin at the University of Portsmouth, with collaborators from Nanjing University.

Kilimanjaro is practically designed for this kind of work. It’s a freestanding stratovolcano – an isolated giant punching straight up from the East African plains at around 800 meters to nearly 5,900 meters.

No surrounding mountain ranges to confuse things. Just one massive cone cycling through every ecosystem imaginable.

Coffee and banana plantations at the base, where over a million people farm the well-watered lower slopes. Then tropical rainforest. Then a heathland belt, alpine desert, and finally the shrinking ice cap at the summit.

Each zone is a distinct climate experiment stacked on top of the last.

The team drew on readings from 22 temperature loggers scattered along two transects – the southwestern Machame route, instrumented since 2004, and the northeastern Rongai route, added in 2012.

Stations sit in everything from the savanna near the town of Moshi (991 meters) to the ice field at 5,799 meters.

That’s among the largest continuous elevation monitoring networks on any tropical mountain in the world.

But ground sensors alone can’t cover the whole mountain. So the researchers merged those readings with satellite data from NASA’s MODIS sensors, which pass over Kilimanjaro four times daily.

They then trained a machine learning model (XGBoost) to predict air temperatures across the entire mountain at one-kilometer resolution.

The model performed remarkably well, explaining 94% of daytime and 95% of nighttime temperature variation, with errors averaging less than 1.8°C.

The trend analysis, covering 2004 to 2019, revealed contrasting temperature changes at different elevations.

Near the summit, daytime temperatures rose by 0.05 to 0.10°C per decade. But between 3,000 and 3,500 meters  – the heathland belt – daytime temperatures actually fell by 0.13 to 0.14°C per decade.

At night, the pattern flipped again. Most elevations experienced slight warming of 0.04 to 0.15°C per decade, while the summit barely budged.

“Climate change does not affect every part of a mountain in the same way,” Pepin said.

“Long-term observations across different elevations help us see these local differences and build a more accurate picture of how mountain environments are changing.”

The cooling on the mid-slopes appears tied to biology as much as physics. Heathland vegetation has been expanding upslope, and denser plant cover changes how the surface handles solar energy.

More leaves mean more evapotranspiration, which diverts the sun’s energy into evaporating water rather than heating the air. More canopy means more shade, less bare ground cooking in the equatorial sun.

“The cooling on the middle slopes coincides with the upslope expansion of the heathland zone,” Mo said.

“This signals that changes in vegetation and land cover may be influencing local temperatures, although other factors are also likely to contribute.”

The paper documents 32 wildfire incidents between 2017 and 2021 around the treeline zone, adding another layer of disturbance.

Fire resets the vegetation clock, strips away canopy, and can produce abrupt changes in local temperature signals.

One of the most striking findings involves the gap between what satellites see and what the air actually feels like.

At the ice field, satellite-measured land surface temperature exceeded air temperature by nearly 17°C during the day.

In the desert zone just below, the difference hit almost 16°C. Meanwhile, in the rainforest, that gap shrank to just 2°C.

The explanation comes down to raw physics. Bare rock and exposed surfaces at high altitude absorb intense equatorial solar radiation and heat up dramatically.

These sunlit surfaces can become much warmer than the air above them.

There’s also a complication. The summit contains both ice and dark rock, and those surfaces behave completely differently under sunlight. Ice stays near freezing while bare rock roasts.

Further down, the news was more encouraging. The rainforest zone showed remarkably little daytime warming over the study period.

Conservation and reforestation may have contributed to this stability, but the researchers say that relationship needs further investigation.

“Our research shows that warming is not necessarily uniform across a mountain, even over relatively short distances,” said study co-author Harold Lovell.

“Combining long-term ground measurements with satellite data helps us identify these differences and could provide a way to study temperature changes in other mountainous regions where weather stations are limited.”

Most evidence for elevation-dependent warming comes from mid-latitude mountains – the Tibetan Plateau, the Alps, the Rockies. There, seasonal snow and big swings in solar radiation drive the patterns.

Tropical mountains play by different rules: persistently intense sunlight, weak temperature seasonality, and energy-balance processes that may produce entirely different warming signatures.

Kilimanjaro could provide a model for studying temperature changes on tropical mountains where long-term weather records remain scarce.

The study is published in the journal npj Climate and Atmospheric Sciences.

#6330. The Next Ice Age Began 2,000 Years Ago. Then, in 1960, Humans Abruptly Ended It.

Ancient moss frozen beneath Baffin Island’s ice tells the story of a glaciation humans snuffed out.

Researchers at Columbia University have pinpointed the summer of 1960 as the moment when a new glacial period, which had already begun, started melting away. They said the blame rests squarely on humans and the surge in greenhouse gases.

In a new study published in the journal Science, the researchers wrote that the newest glacial period (often colloquially called an ice age) began 2,000 years ago, even though it would have taken about 30,000 years for anyone to really notice. Human activity cut it short in 1960.

“It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen—and yet it stopped,” Nicolas Young, a geochemist at the Columbia Climate School, said in a statement from Columbia University. “It’s a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.”

To gather their data, the team studied what remains of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. At its peak roughly 20,000 years ago, the ice sheet stretched from the Arctic Circle down to Illinois and was two miles thick in places. It shrank to its smallest size about 3,000 years ago, then started growing again about 2,000 years ago.

“People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” Young said of the ice sheet. He noted that a piece of it survives today as the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island in the Canadian territory of Nunavut, and that this remnant is still about the size of Delaware. Because the ice cap is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it, it doesn’t slide, so it preserves the vegetation underneath instead of scraping it away. When the ice expands, it entombs the plants it covers. When it recedes, it exposes them again, allowing the team to sample the moss and date it using radiocarbon dating.

“If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants,” Young said. “You’re actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin.”

That timeline is critical, according to Joerg Schaefer, also a Columbia climate geochemist. “We have a decent understanding of how this enormous ice sheet grew and disappeared over thousands of years from proxy records, but catching the start of this process with direct observations is new,” Schaefer said. “Our approach helped us see the first steps of ice-sheet growth preserved in the landscape. It gave us a rare opportunity to understand how re-glaciation begins and how the Laurentide Ice Sheet reforms.”

Technically, Earth has been in the Late Cenozoic Ice Age for about 34 million years, the researchers said. Within that span, the planet swings between glacial periods and warmer interglacial periods, and conventionally we have been in an interglacial since the last glacial period ended roughly 11,700 years ago. The new research challenges that framework by arguing that the first renewed growth of an ice sheet equals the start of a glacial period, “marking the onset of the next glaciation.” That period didn’t last long, however. The ice cap reached its maximum extent around 1960, when summer warming caused a “negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation.”

In other words, Earth’s climate had warmed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap lost more ice in the summer of 1960 than it gained the previous winter, effectively ending the next glaciation. “The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate,” the authors wrote.

The team expects the ice cap to vanish within a few centuries. Without that icy foundation, it will be harder for new ice to build up. As a result, scientists can’t say when (or where) the next glaciation might occur, especially while greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere remain high.

Young described what the ice cap’s loss will mean: “That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good,” he said. “What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6329. Crowds leave a hidden seismic signature beneath a city

Seismic recordings reveal how crowd size and coordinated movements shape ground vibrations, offering clues that could help monitor large gatherings.

Every time you take a step, you shake the ground. Not by much – a fraction of a micron – but seismometers don’t care about “much.” They care about patterns.

And when 11,000 people march through the streets of Troy, New York, or 100,000 pilgrims gather at a hilltop shrine in northern Israel, those tiny individual tremors add up to something a seismologist can read like sheet music.

Asaf Inbal from Tel Aviv University has done exactly that. He analyzed seismic recordings from Tokyo schoolyards, American protest marches, and an Israeli pilgrimage.

That helped him build the first large-scale framework connecting crowd size and behavior to the vibrations they leave in the ground.

The strongest crowd-generated seismic energy lands in the 1–2 hertz band, which lines up neatly with the natural rhythm of human walking.

That’s been suspected for a while, but Inbal nailed it down with data from roughly 300 accelerometers belonging to Tokyo’s Metropolitan Seismic Observation Network (MeSO-Net).

Most of those sensors sit in schoolyards – an accident of infrastructure planning that turned out to be a gift for studying how feet translate into waveforms.

The Tokyo data revealed something unexpectedly precise.

Seismic amplitudes spiked every weekday morning around 8 a.m. when school started. They then dipped at exactly 10:00 for morning break, again at noon for lunch, and once more at 3 p.m. for afternoon tea.

The network was essentially reading the school bell schedule through the ground. Even the pre-dawn hours told a story. A mysterious 5 a.m. amplitude peak turned out to match early morning truck traffic routes through the Chiba Prefecture, confirmed by independent freight data.

The real surprise came when Inbal plotted crowd size against seismic signal strength across five orders of magnitude. The size varied from a handful of schoolchildren to a hundred thousand pilgrims.

Two completely different scaling relationships emerged.

For Tokyo schools, the correlation between crowd size and ground shaking was essentially flat. A school with 1,200 students barely registered more than one with 400.

The correlation coefficient was just 0.08, indicating almost no relationship.

But for outdoor gatherings – protests, rallies, marches, pilgrimages – the relationship was steep and tight, with a correlation coefficient of 0.77 and a scaling slope of 0.81.

The difference isn’t just about numbers. It’s about coordination.

“We found that crowds engaged in coordinated activity tend to generate stronger seismic signals than similarly sized crowds engaged in uncoordinated activity,” Inbal explained.

“More surprisingly, the seismic amplitudes associated with coordinated activity increase more rapidly with crowd size.”

“This suggests that seismic excitation does not depend simply on the number of people. The type of activity also matters, and its influence becomes increasingly significant for larger crowds.”

Children on a playground move in different directions and at different rhythms, producing footfalls that overlap irregularly.

Marching, rhythmic chanting, jumping, and dancing can produce more coordinated ground vibrations.

That coordination may help explain why some gatherings generate stronger seismic signals than others of similar size.

Inbal analyzed two landmark events in detail. The 2020 Black Lives Matter march in Troy, New York, drew approximately 11,000 people.

Its strongest seismic amplifications showed up between 1.5 and 2 Hz, with short-term bursts lasting minutes to hours rather than a clean onset and stop.

The 2021 annual pilgrimage at Meron, Israel – attended by roughly 100,000 people – hit even harder, with amplifications between 1.5 and 2.5 Hz and an additional peak between 3 and 4.5 Hz, likely from rhythmic jumping and dancing.

That Meron pilgrimage ended in catastrophe: a crowd crush killed 45 people. A subsequent state commission of inquiry concluded that the disaster could have been avoided if crowd sizes had been known in real time.

Inbal borrowed a concept from earthquake science to formalize his findings. Just as seismologists use magnitude scales to characterize earthquakes, he developed ground-motion scaling relationships for human crowds.

“Because the seismic signals depend not only on the number of people but also on how they move, I sometimes call these scaling relationships the ‘People’s Magnitude,’” he said.

The approach required some seismological housekeeping. Surface waves generated by stomping feet decay proportionally to one over the square root of distance.

So Inbal corrected all his amplification factors for geometrical spreading before comparing events recorded at different ranges.

He also set strict quality filters. Events had to produce amplification factors above 1.5 for at least 900 consecutive seconds. They also had to fall within specific distance thresholds of the nearest seismometer.

Of the 385 outdoor gatherings that met the distance criteria, 100 passed the amplitude and duration tests.

What drew Inbal down this path was a collision between two of his interests. His earlier work on urban microseismicity – understanding how city noise interferes with earthquake detection – led him to MeSO-Net data.

And as he puts it, this in turn “led me to consider whether seismic data could be used to characterize ground motion generated by human crowds more broadly.”

Along the way, he studied the physics of collective crowd behavior and found “intriguing parallels” with his own work.

“Both studies suggest that interactions among people can have measurable collective consequences,” he noted.

“I’m used to thinking about how interactions between faults manifest themselves in seismic signals, so I found the idea that interactions among people could also leave a measurable seismic signature particularly appealing.”

The practical implications circle back to Meron.

If crowd-generated seismic signals scale predictably with both size and behavioral state, then existing seismic networks could, in theory, monitor large gatherings in real time.

“Ultimately, I’d like to understand whether changes in a crowd’s seismic signature could reveal transitions in its collective behavior, potentially even before those changes become apparent through conventional monitoring,” Inbal concluded.

The study is published in the journal Seismological Research Letters.

#6328. Before a baby is born, a mother’s brain holds clues to their bond

A small study links bonding with an unborn baby to more coordinated activity in specific brain regions of mothers.

A pregnant woman may imagine what her baby looks like or pause to enjoy the feeling of the baby moving.

Researchers have studied this early bond for decades, yet relatively little is known about what’s happening in the mother’s brain as it forms.

Late in pregnancy, women who reported more anticipation of and interaction with their baby had more closely matched electrical rhythms between certain parts of the brain.

The new study suggests that parts of the bond are already reflected in the brain before birth.

Kathy Ayala of Yale’s Interdepartmental Neuroscience Program conducted the study with colleagues.

The senior researcher was Helena Rutherford, an associate professor in the Yale Child Study Center.

The team recorded brain activity once in each of 35 women in their third trimester. The results show a link at one moment in pregnancy, not proof that one thing causes the other.

Researchers call this early connection maternal-fetal attachment, though the word attachment is debated.

Classic attachment theory uses it for a child seeking care from another person, while here it means the mother’s one-way emotional bond with the fetus.

Earlier studies have linked a stronger bond during pregnancy to more sensitive caregiving after birth and to more responsive interactions between mothers and babies.

Each woman rated 18 statements from “almost never” to “almost always.”

Six covered anticipation, such as “I wonder what the baby looks like now,” and six covered interaction, such as “I enjoy feeling the baby move.”

The last six covered differentiation, a mother’s sense of the baby as a separate person, such as “I think the baby already has a personality.”

Each six-statement part had a top score of 24 points, and the group’s averages ran from about 18.7 to 19.6 points.

The volunteers were recruited through flyers and word of mouth around New Haven, Connecticut.

They were 28 years old on average and nearly 37 weeks pregnant, and 22 of them had never given birth before.

Each woman wore a net of 128 sensors, soaked beforehand in a warm salt solution.

In a dim, quiet room, she spent three 30-second stretches with her eyes closed, alternating with three with her eyes open.

The sensors recorded an EEG, the brain’s electrical activity as picked up from the scalp. Only the eyes-closed recordings were analyzed, because earlier work found them steadier.

The team focused on alpha waves, a rhythm that rises and falls 8 to 13 times per second. Alpha activity has been tied to attention, memory, and holding back unwanted responses.

The researchers measured coherence: how closely the alpha rhythm at one spot on the scalp rises and falls with the rhythm at another spot. It’s like checking whether two people clapping keep the same beat.

Four pairs of spots were compared. Two ran across the head, at the front and near the top and back, and two ran from front to back on each side.

Two of those pairs showed links with the questionnaire.

Women whose alpha rhythms over the left front and left back of the head were more closely in step scored higher on anticipation and on interaction.

So did women whose rhythms over the left and right front of the head were more closely in step.

The links held after the researchers accounted for how far along each woman was and whether she had given birth before.

The pair across the back of the head and the pair on the right side showed no link with either score.

Each of these positive associations met the threshold for statistical significance, though only narrowly.

Women who scored high on one part of the questionnaire tended to score high on all three. Yet differentiation showed only weak links with the brain measures, and none passed that test.

A 2022 study offers one possible explanation.

It measured women’s brains before and after pregnancy and found that increases in coordination within a large set of connected regions, called the default mode network, were linked to differentiation.

The 2022 study tracked changes across a whole pregnancy, while the new one measured each brain once.

Ayala’s team suggested that differentiation may depend on longer-term brain changes, while alpha coherence may reflect a woman’s engagement with the fetus in the moment.

Or, the authors wrote, 35 women may have been too few to detect a link with differentiation.

A 2023 study that Rutherford co-authored found that alpha coherence between the left front and left back of the head falls from pregnancy to the period after birth.

Its authors read the drop as a loosening of the brain’s tendency to hold back responses, which may help new mothers react to a baby’s signals.

If lower coherence after birth helps mothers respond, is higher coherence during pregnancy a problem?

According to Ayala’s team, not necessarily. Pregnancy changes the brain in large ways.

A 2025 study found that gray matter, the tissue that holds the bodies of nerve cells, shrinks during pregnancy and partly recovers after birth.

The steepest declines came in the default mode network and in networks linking the front and top of the brain. Ayala’s team described any tie between those changes and its own results as speculative.

Still, the authors suggest that higher coherence during pregnancy may reflect a brain state suited to preparing for parenthood.

The later drop may support a different job, responding to the infant.

The study was small, and it captured each woman at a single point late in pregnancy.

The authors found it surprising that the links didn’t differ between first-time mothers and women who had given birth before.

Earlier work had found that first-time mothers report a stronger bond during pregnancy.

With only 22 women in one group and 13 in the other, the study may have been too small to detect a difference.

Future studies should also measure mental health, including depression and anxiety, the authors wrote.

Because the women weren’t followed past birth, the study can’t say whether those with the most closely matched rhythms cared for their newborns differently.

The researchers want future studies to follow women from before conception into the period after birth, which could show whether the bond or the brain rhythms change first.

The full study was published in the Journal of Neuroendocrinology.

#6327. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Sanders: This shift happened in a very, very short amount of time, and it has big implications, both good and bad.

Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time, and somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: Farid tells me about some of his research, which asks people to decide whether something, like a voice or a video, is real.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? It’s really cool.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6326. Scientists Cracked the Code on a 400-Year-Old Padlock. What It Was Protecting Is Still a Mystery.

An engineer peered inside the brass lock and found a four-letter puzzle to open it. Unfortunately, it’s not locking anything anymore.

A 16th-century brass padlock that secured treasure aboard the Ann Francis—an English merchant vessel used for smuggling—went down with the ship when it wrecked off the Welsh coast in a wild December 1583 storm. The padlock then lay hidden in the sand of Margam Beach for centuries. Even after a metal detectorist found it among the wreck’s hoard, its combination stayed a mystery—until now.

“It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery,” said David Williams, a research associate at Cardiff University, in a statement.

Williams works at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University’s School of Engineering, where he typically uses his skills to study anatomy. This time, however, he looked deep inside the padlock, using micro-CT scanning to examine its internal mechanism without damaging it. The scans revealed the four-letter combination that opened the lock: ANCE.

“By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination,” Williams said. “We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us.”

After Williams sent the combination to the experts at Amgueddfa Cymru–Museum Wales, which cares for the Ann Francis treasure hoard, he could only wait to find out whether it worked. “Getting the message that we’d cracked it was incredibly satisfying,” he said.

Alastair Willis, the museum’s senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy, said Elizabethan combination locks aren’t uncommon in Britain, but this one was in exceptional condition. Because the lock came from the Ann Francis, it can be dated precisely, which made it a “unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve.”

Still, questions remain. “Of course, now we’ve solved it we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner,” Willis said. The team is also left to wonder exactly what the lock secured.

The lock’s modern story began in 1996, when metal detectorist Peter Hughes discovered the wreck and part of the treasure it carried. For the next 21 years, Hughes kept returning to the beach, uncovering artifacts whenever dredging and storms stripped away layers of sand. His finds include rare gold coins from the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, a boatswain’s whistle and other 16th-century coins. Among them was the padlock, which he found in 1999.

“When I found the lock, I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition,” he said. “When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief. I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things from the treasure chest it once locked.”

Experts can only guess at what the chest held. Hughes found a collection of Spanish silver coins and two coin weights near the padlock, so the lock may have protected those objects. Or it may have secured a chest of other valuables, such as documents, that didn’t survive the wreck or the centuries that followed.

The lock and the rest of the Ann Francis hoard are on display in the Tides of Treasure exhibition at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea.

That leaves one last mystery: What, if anything, did ANCE mean?

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6325. What makes people pay more for sustainable products? Study identifies a key factor

Why don’t green values always lead to greener purchases? A new study explores how enjoyment and practicality shape willingness to pay more.

Here’s a paradox that should keep sustainability marketers awake at night. Consumers who genuinely care about the environment and say they’d happily pay extra for eco-friendly products often don’t.

They walk past the biofuel, ignore the recycled-fiber T-shirt, and go home with whatever was cheapest and most practical.

The gap between what people believe and what they actually buy is called the sustainability value-behavior gap. A new study may have now found one of its key mechanisms.

Whether a product feels enjoyable or primarily functional may help explain the gap.

Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland found that hedonic attitudes – the sense that a sustainable product is fun, exciting, or delightful – act as a bridge between people’s green values and their wallets.

Utilitarian attitudes – the cold calculus of price, efficiency, and practicality – do the opposite. They widen the gap.

The research team, led by Jani Holopainen and doctoral researcher Jyri Hoffrén, ran three studies using a demographically representative panel of Finnish and Dutch citizens.

The first tested their theoretical model on 461 participants. The results were clear: sustainable consumption values strongly predicted willingness to pay a premium for green products.

But when hedonic attitudes entered the picture that relationship got even stronger.

“Consumers who value sustainable consumption are more willing to pay a premium, particularly when a product offers positive emotional and user experiences. Enjoyment helps translate sustainability values into actual consumption behavior,” Hoffrén said.

In the base model, sustainable values alone explained 47 percent of the variance in willingness to pay a premium.

Adding hedonic and utilitarian attitudes as moderators nudged the model’s explanatory power to nearly 48 percent.

That’s not a dramatic gain in raw statistical terms. Still, the interaction effects were significant and, more importantly, pointed in opposite directions.

The second study asked whether this was just a snapshot or something durable.

The researchers followed 239 participants over two years, measuring their sustainable consumption values and attitudes at one point and their actual purchasing behavior two years later.

The pattern held. Values predicted behavior across the two-year gap, and hedonic attitudes strengthened that link while utilitarian attitudes weakened it.

Values tend to be stable, but attitudes fluctuate. The fact that hedonic attitudes measured at time one still amplified the values-to-behavior connection at time two suggests something deeper than a fleeting mood.

The results suggest that enjoyment may help people act on their sustainability values, while a stronger focus on practical considerations may weaken that connection.

The third study broke the question apart across three wood-based bioproducts that sit at different points on the pleasure-to-practicality spectrum: a bioplastic water bottle, a T-shirt made from wood-based fabric, and a wood-based biofuel.

The bioplastic bottle was the star. Both effects showed up clearly – hedonic attitudes boosted willingness to pay, utilitarian attitudes dragged it down.

This aligns with earlier research suggesting that ecological packaging is inherently perceived as hedonic. People find it appealing, novel, and satisfying to hold. That emotional connection does real commercial work.

The T-shirt fell in the middle. Utilitarian attitudes still suppressed willingness to pay, but the hedonic boost disappeared.

The biofuel landed at the utilitarian extreme, and the results were stark. The negative utilitarian interaction was the strongest across all three products.

People who evaluated biofuel through the lens of price and efficiency were significantly less likely to pay a premium, even when they held strong sustainability values. The hedonic interaction was not even statistically significant.

The findings also raise a potential concern about greenwashing. The researchers suggest that emphasizing enjoyment could make consumers less critical of environmental claims.

“Companies should consider sustainability as part of a product’s overall value. If product marketing emphasizes enjoyment without genuine experiential benefits, it may lose credibility,” Hoffrén said.

“For utilitarian products, consumers are also quick to scrutinise whether the environmental benefits are genuine.”

Enjoyment may help legitimate sustainable products attract buyers, but it could also give misleading environmental claims an advantage.

Policymakers eyeing greenwashing regulations might want to pay particular attention to products marketed at the intersection of sustainability and pleasure.

The study was published in a forestry economics journal for a reason.

Wood-based bioproducts – an expanding category that includes bioplastics, textiles, and biofuels – face exactly this dilemma.

For the bioplastic bottle, enjoyment strengthened the link between sustainability values and willingness to pay extra. For biofuel, practical considerations weakened that link most strongly.

For the wood products industry, the lesson is that environmental credentials alone won’t move units. The product has to feel good in someone’s hand, or on their body, or in their daily routine.

“This finding helps explain the value-behavior gap. Consumers may consider sustainability important but decide not to buy a product if its price, practicality, or perceived benefits fail to meet their expectations,” Hoffrén concluded.

The study is published in the journal Forest Policy and Economics.

The reentry of NASA's dead Swift space telescope is the end of an era for rapid-response space science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's the end of an era: NASA's Swift telescope has reached the conclusion of its nearly 22-year mission, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after studying some of the universe's most powerful and mysterious events.

According to NASA, the spacecraft reentered the atmosphere at "7:39 a.m. EST Wednesday over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, at approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude." NASA expected most of the telescope's structure to burn up during its passage through Earth's atmosphere, estimating a 1-in-2,100 chance of any surviving debris falling over a populated area. No damage or injuries have been reported.

Weighing approximately 3,200 pounds (1,450 kilograms), the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was initially designed for a two-year mission, but it far exceeded expectations. Over two decades, Swift became an important tool in the study of gamma-ray bursts, supernovas, black holes and other cosmic phenomena.

Launched in November 2004, Swift was designed to detect gamma-ray bursts, powerful explosions that occur throughout the universe. Its three onboard telescopes let scientists observe cosmic events across different wavelengths, including ultraviolet, optical and X-ray light. The telescope could swivel to focus on different sky targets in a matter of minutes, allowing it to rapidly follow up on sudden events like supernova explosions.

NASA estimates that Swift's scientific observations have contributed to approximately 7,000 research papers, leaving behind an extensive collection that scientists can continue studying for years.

Swift's return was driven by atmospheric drag, which eventually slowed the spacecraft and caused its orbit to decay. Increased solar activity intensified the drag, thus accelerating the space telescope's descent toward Earth.

Earlier this year, NASA explored an ambitious rescue mission to extend Swift's operational life. In August 2026, a privately developed robotic spacecraft built by Katalyst Space Technologies was intended to rendezvous with Swift and boost it into a higher orbit. However, the mission failed after launching, leaving the observatory on its path toward reentry.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

NASA officially ended Swift's scientific operations on Oct. 20 after its declining altitude made observations too difficult. For NASA and the broader astronomy community, Swift's story is a reminder that even missions designed to last just a few years can fundamentally change our understanding of our universe.

#6323. A lost sea channel shaped this striking corner of Cyprus

A satellite image of Cyprus reveals how ancient islands joined to form the Akrotiri Peninsula, enclosing a salt lake once open to the sea.

A shallow salt lake at the southern edge of Cyprus marks a place where the Mediterranean once flowed between two islands.

Today, strips of land join those islands together, leaving a coastal landscape that still carries the outline of its watery past.

The Akrotiri Peninsula offers a striking reminder that even an island’s shape is temporary.

Rivers, shifting shorelines, and rising rock helped build this southern tip of Cyprus, connecting land that once stood apart.

On October 10, 2026, Landsat 8 captured images of the peninsula’s sandy margins and the lake enclosed between them.

Behind that modern view lies a story spanning ancient ocean floors, migrating flamingos, and a cape whose name recalls a legendary arrival of cats.

Akrotiri Salt Lake occupies a former arm of the Mediterranean.

Its enclosure happened gradually, as sediment accumulated along two routes between Cyprus and a smaller island to the south.

These natural connections are known as tombolos: deposits of sand, gravel, or other sediment that link an island to another landmass.

At Akrotiri, two such bridges helped turn separate islands into a single peninsula.

The western connection formed first. About 50,000 years ago, gravel and sand delivered by the Kouris River began building the tombolo on that side.

The eastern connection developed later, extending south from Cyprus.

Geologists place the final separation of the lagoon from the open Mediterranean within the past 2,000 years.

That difference in timing gives the landscape an unusual perspective.

Although the rocks beneath Cyprus record tens of millions of years, the closure that helped define this lake occurred within human history.

The two land bridges also explain why the lake sits where it does. Rather than forming in an isolated inland basin, it occupies space left between growing coastal connections.

Its position preserves evidence of the channel even though the surrounding land now provides an unbroken route onto the peninsula.

Long before those sediment bridges formed, the material that would become Cyprus was taking shape underwater.

About 90 million years ago, during the Late Cretaceous, molten rock emerged from the seafloor and cooled into new oceanic crust.

Tectonic forces eventually pushed portions of that crust upward, bringing formerly submerged rock above the waves.

The Troodos Mountains preserve remnants of this ancient oceanic material.

Geologists call the rock assemblage an ophiolite, a term associated with the snakelike appearance of some of its mottled green rocks.

The peninsula’s southern portion has a different geological background.

During the much later Miocene epoch, marine deposits accumulated around the emerging island, including chalk, limestone, and marl.

Later uplift raised some of this younger material into a smaller island offshore.

River sediment and marine deposits eventually filled parts of the intervening channel, creating the connections visible in the peninsula’s present shape.

The lake now follows a seasonal rhythm. Water typically returns in late autumn and winter, while summer brings drying.

Those winter waters have historically supported large gatherings of flamingos, with overwintering numbers averaging about 4,000 birds.

The birds come to feed on small creatures such as fairy shrimp. These shrimp contain carotenoids, pigments that contribute to the flamingos’ familiar pink coloration.

Recent counts offer a more sobering picture. News reports put the lake’s wintering flamingo population at just 30 birds in 2025, a sharp departure from its historical abundance.

The satellite scene captures the setting for this seasonal gathering.

The birds themselves, and the changes in their numbers, belong to a smaller scale of observation that adds another layer to the landscape’s story.

On the southeastern peninsula, Cape Gata introduces a different animal connection. Its name means Cape Cat in Greek.

According to legend, a severe fourth-century drought left Cyprus struggling with snakes. Empress Helena, the mother of Constantine the Great, responded by arranging for cats to arrive from Egypt.

The story places some of those cats near what became the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats, where monks supposedly encouraged them to hunt snakes.

The tale survives alongside a continuing tradition of caring for cats at the monastery.

Seen together, the lake, land bridges, and cape reveal several histories sharing one small stretch of coast.

Ancient seabed became an island, sediment closed a channel, and people attached stories to the land that emerged.

The shoreline in this image is the latest chapter in a landscape still shaped by water.
