#6286. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6284. 21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

We’ll never forget the first time we visited New York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

In fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

December is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

If you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

We once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

Why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

We’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

Where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

We were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

While Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

We thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

Sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like New York City at Christmas.

Why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

We’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

Why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

We love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

We’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

Walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

Why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

We had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

Why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A New Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

We went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks shows are fantastic.

Why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

Here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

We’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

One of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

Why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

This was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

For the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

Yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

December is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

We hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you plan your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?

#6283. It’s Almost a Year Since the FCC Banned Most New Consumer Drones: We Rank the Ones Still on Sale

Almost no new drones launched in the U.S. in 2026. These are the best old models still flying (and on sale) from brands we trust.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The FCC’s decision to ban the import of foreign-made drones last December effectively ground the entire category to a halt. Only a handful of new drones hit stores this year, mostly because they received approval prior to the ban, so the options we have when we need a new one have stayed more or less the same since then. Outside the U.S., companies like DJI are still putting out new drones: As they move on to bigger and better, we can’t help but wonder if or when we’ll start to see supplies of U.S.-approved models dry up.

So far, things seem pretty stable. Many of our favorites remain available, and there are a few we’re still hoping to test. We’re hoping that some domestic brands pick up the slack and start innovating in the field, but, for now, we’ve decided to keep a running “still-fly” list of the ones you can still buy in case supplies start to thin out.

To be clear, this isn’t a comprehensive list of every possible available drone. (Frankly, that wouldn’t be helpful. Not every drone is worth monitoring.) Instead, think of it as merely a long list of drones, both tested and untested, that we’re keeping an eye on as viable options in case our top recommendations go out of stock. I’ve also ranked these options, roughly, based on their core specs, including camera quality, battery power, range, and price.

DJI’s U.S.-available flagship drone, the Mavic 4 Pro, offers perhaps the best camera capabilities and clarity of footage of any consumer-grade drone out there right now. It has three distinct cameras: a 28mm lens for crisp details and low-light shooting, a 70mm medium tele lens for portraits and medium-range shooting, and a 168mm tele lens for long-range shooting. They operate on a 360-degree gimbal, so you have full control to record stills and video up close or from a distance, and at any angle.

Beyond the cameras, the drone comes with a powerful motor and long-lasting battery that allows you to fly in windy conditions and still come home with stable, clear footage. We don’t expect the average person to need three high-resolution cameras, 51 minutes of battery, and a top speed of 50 mph, but if you’re more than a hobby flyer, it’s hard to find a better choice.

One of the most affordable and easy-to-fly drones from DJI, the original DJI Neo is an older model that’s perfect for a beginner who wants to learn the ropes. The caged propellers are very helpful to pilots who lack a certain level of nuance with the controls and are prone to crashing. The cage prevents damage to the propellers or the motor.

At the same time, in our own testing, the Neo was exceptionally easy to steer with smooth, responsive controls and several preset flight modes that fly the drone automatically in specific patterns. While you can’t expect professional-grade footage, the 4K camera will be more than enough for casual fliers.

I’ve rated this drone so highly because the price tag is so low. There is a newer version, the Neo 2, with better specs, and normally I’d recommend going with the newer model to reduce the chances that DJI might stop supporting the Neo with security updates. Given the circumstances, though, future-proofing is less of a factor here. And it’s very hard to pass up a drone of this quality at such a low price.

The Autel Evo II is a thermal imaging drone, primarily designed for search and rescue operations, power plant inspections, and even to assist firefighters. In theory, it could also be a useful tool for hunters looking to identify wildlife from a distance. Its thermal imaging camera can detect a subject from up to 100 meters away, even if they’re visually obscured by brush or obstacles.

It’s also quite powerful: The Evo II can fly up to 45 mph, so it can reach the edge of its nine-mile range in just 12 minutes. With 16x zoom, it can also scan nearby areas for small thermal signatures with relative ease.

Between its specific use case and very high price tag, this is not a drone for the average person. But it should be very capable in the right hands.

Like the DJI Neo, the HoverAir X1 is a small camera drone that’s both durable and fairly affordable, which makes it a great choice for beginners. The biggest difference is that the X1 is made for truly novice pilots who don’t trust their skills at all.

While you can fly it manually, the drone comes loaded with a number of preprogrammed flight patterns and flying modes that don’t require any piloting at all. The auto-follow feature allows you to essentially launch and forget about it. At a top speed of around 15 miles per hour, you can bike or even snowboard with the drone to capture footage.

At the same time, the propellers are protected by the wraparound frame made of a flexible polymer. So, in the case of a crash, no harm, no foul. I personally love the foldable design. Folded down, I’m able to fit the entire drone in my pocket.

The drone we recommend for most people, regardless of experience or use case, DJI Mini 4K, is a decently affordable jack-of-all-trades.

For $300, the Mini 4K has a ton of great features that empower both new and veteran users, including pre-programmed routes, one-touch takeoff, and an automatic return-to-home system. The GPS-enabled return home system is a popular feature on many drones but one not common on a model in this price range.

That said, the Mini is more than a mere fly-toy. It features a 4K camera and level 5 wind resistance, allowing it to handle in gusts up to 24 miles per hour so you can film on gusty days. The battery life is short, but functional: With the three batteries you get in this set, you should get over 90 minutes of flight time, so it’s set for leisurely flight or most short-term survey and recording tasks.

There aren’t many drone brands with a reputation for making reliable “prosumer” drones that deliver the kind of build quality and performance you want for serious projects at a price hobbyists can afford. As a result, DJI has become a singularly dominant brand, but there are brands like Potensic out there cultivating a similar track record, even if their footprints are smaller.

The Atom SE is another great starter, given the price and solid maneuverability. It’s a very solid drone with a lot of cool features and few significant downsides. It can fly continuously for over 30 minutes on a full charge, films in 4K, and has a few programmable flight modes for hands-free flying.

Another unique feature is the GPS auto return: No matter where you are, you can press a button and the drone will begin flying to you. This particular SE kit comes with a controller that is compatible with your smartphone for integrated flying and real-time footage.

With a more powerful motor and a greater selection of preprogrammed flight patterns than the classic X1, the X1 Promax is a definite upgrade on the classic X1 for folks looking for a bit more power and a wider array of features, even as they’re still getting the hang of drone control.

Much like the X1, the Promax is both supremely portable and durable. The protective cage around the propellers means it can take a ton of pretty hefty crashes without causing any serious damage. At the same time, it has the same foldable build so it fits perfectly in a pocket. That makes it an awesome action cam alternative for outdoor adventurers who want a remote cameraman to help film extreme sports like snowboarding or dirt biking.

Like the X1 Promax, the Potensic Atom 2 drone offers a more feature-rich (and expensive) step up from the brand’s basic Atom SE. The drone has an incredibly clear 4K camera, over 30 minutes of flight time, and a pretty impressive top speed of close to 36 mph. In comparison to the SE, the Atom 2 makes some notable improvements. These include filming at a higher frame rate, offering more than double the range, providing a three-axis gimbal for greater video stability, and including AI digital tracking for better hands-free flying.

During testing, I was really impressed by how responsive it feels in the air. I was a novice pilot when I used it, but was able to fly it with more finesse and nuance than many of the drones I’d tried before, including some more expensive models. And it’s easy to fly the Atom 2 by pairing it with your phone, though the kit I’ve highlighted here comes with a dedicated controller with a large view screen.

If you want clearer, cleaner footage and a bit more power from your motor, this is your answer over the Atom SE.

The DJI Neo 2 is another upgraded riff on a core favorite of mine, with some notable upgrades and a substantially higher price tag. Unsurprisingly, this upgraded model features upgraded performance across the board, including stronger wind resistance, faster tracking speed, and two-axis stability for smoother video while hovering or flying. It’s also still quite durable, with enclosed propellers that provide extra protection against crashes that might otherwise cause damage to delicate parts of the drone.

The Atom 3 is Potensic’s newest drone, and the brand’s flagship model. Its best quality is its tremendous battery life, up to 50 minutes of continuous flight on a single charge. The camera also gets an upgrade, with a three-axis gimbal for more control and better stability while shooting on the move, even in high winds.

It also boasts a solid top speed of 36 mph, a 4K camera with an AI-enhanced night mode for better clarity during night shoots, and a nearly 10-mile range, which is notably larger than both the Atom SE and Atom 2.

The improvements on the Atom 3 won’t be huge for the average flier, but could definitely make a difference for those shooting serious footage or who want to fly for a lot longer before swapping batteries. If the Atom SE is for the new pilots, and the Atom 2 is for moderate hobbyists looking for a premium camera, then the Atom 3 is a serious upgrade for expert pilots who need both precision flight control and a prosumer-grade camera.

Easily the most notable new drone of 2026, the Antigravity A1 is a high-end camera drone built for speed and aerial acrobatics. The controls include a pair of viewfinder goggles that give you the full UAV pilot experience, which should make for more thrilling flights. (And more precise recording if you’re using it for creative work.) Meanwhile, the hand controls blend conventional button inputs with motion controls for smooth turns and nuanced, intuitive flight control.

Candidly, I haven’t tested the A1 yet, but I’m hoping to soon. It’s an interesting and exciting take that represents everything we’d like to see when and if the drone market restabilizes.

Holy Stone isn’t as well known as many of the other brands on this list. The brand makes affordable drones with functional controls and solid design. The HS360E isn’t quite as impressive as DJI’s Mini or the HoverAir X1 on paper, but you’re still getting a 4K camera drone with some premium features at a very reasonable price.

Another drone that lets you see through the camera using display goggles, the DJI Avata 2 is ideal for acrobatic flying and high-speed video on a bit more of a budget. The goggles offer real-time POV footage of what your drone sees while the one-handed control works using the motion of your wrist to turn or accelerate.

What sets this drone apart from most others is how capable it is of genuinely acrobatic flight. It can flip, roll, or even drift 180 degrees with ease, so you can pilot it hard and with intention without fear of going beyond its means.

With a close-to-45-minute flight time and both medium- and wide-angle cameras, this is a great drone for long filming sessions over landscapes. In fact, the drone even comes with 45 gigabytes of internal storage so you can save tons of footage directly to the device without worrying about uploading it to a cloud-based storage system.

The Air 3S also has omnidirectional obstacle sensing so it will make adjustments to avoid crashing into walls or trees even when flying at high speeds.

I wouldn’t expect this drone to win in a race, but a bubble drone seems like a pretty good time if you’ve got young kids, and it’s the only one I’ve seen from a notable brand with this kind of a feature. The HS320 bubble drone is built with an internal bubble machine that sprays hundreds of bubbles as it flies over you.

Notably, this drone does not feature a camera. That it’s more of a toy than a tool works in its favor, I think, because that keeps the price down. At under $100, this is a great way to liven up an afternoon in the backyard, but also a really easy entry point for folks who want to learn how to fly.

A high-status burial surprised archaeologists when they discovered leprosy in a man's bones from the fifth century.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists investigating the genomes of a dozen people buried in an abandoned Roman-era settlement in northwestern Germany have discovered a surprising organism lurking in one man's remains: a rare strain of Mycobacterium leprae, which causes leprosy.

This strain of leprosy has never been seen in this part of Europe before, which hints that the individual had traveled and interacted with people from across the Roman world. The man was buried in a wooden boat surrounded by unusual objects, indicating he was a high-status person, according to a research study.

"The results were particularly striking in the case of one individual," study co-author Ben Krause-Kyora, an archaeologist at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) at Kiel University in Germany, said in a Nov. 3 statement. "He could, for example, have been a mercenary in the Roman army who later settled between the Elbe and the Weser [rivers]."

In the study, published online Oct. 15 in the journal iScience, Krause-Kyora and colleagues analyzed the genomes of people buried at the coastal settlement of Fallward. The settlement originated in the first century B.C. but gradually declined and became a cemetery by the fifth century A.D. Among the 200 cremation burials and 60 inhumation burials originally excavated in the 1990s was a distinctive grave made from a wooden boat.

The oak boat was over 13 feet (4 meters) long and sealed with a roof-like structure, the researchers said. It held the skeleton of a man who was about 50 years old when he died some time between A.D. 425 and 450. His grave goods included a small box shaped like a water bird, an ornate chair or throne carved out of alder wood, a bronze basin and a maple stool with a hunting scene and a runic inscription. The maritime artifacts coupled with the man's well-developed upper arm bones suggest he may have worked as a fisherman or boatman just before he died, the researchers wrote.

"The grave goods placed in the tomb aroused particular scientific interest," study co-author Hauke Jöns, an archaeologist at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research, said in the statement. "The man possessed a late Roman military belt, which suggested that the deceased had had connections across great distances."

Archaeologists found a chair made from the trunk of an alder tree near the man's burial. The chair was likely a symbol of authority or power.

To learn more about this unusual burial and to determine where the man was from, researchers analyzed his DNA.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Genetic analyses confirm that a man buried at Fallward originated from the Danube region," study first author Daniel Myburgh, an ancient DNA researcher at IKMB, said in the statement. "He was also infected with a very rare leprosy pathogen."

The researchers found the DNA of the bacterium M. leprae in one of the man's teeth and in a foot bone. Because the leprosy DNA was so well preserved, the researchers were able to narrow down the strain that had infected him. This strain of leprosy may have evolved in Egypt around the fourth to second centuries B.C. and had never before been found in Central or Northern Europe, according to the statement.

But the man showed no signs of leprosy lesions in his skeleton, the researchers said. Leprosy first attacks the nerves and skin, but it can eventually eat away at the bones of the skeleton, particularly affecting the nose, jaw, hands and feet.

"Leprosy is a chronic disease," study co-author Almut Nebel, a biologist at IKMB, said in the statement. "Either he was affected by an asymptomatic form of the disease, or the disease had so far only affected soft tissues. He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease."

While the researchers don't know exactly what happened in this man's life, they suggested he might have been a mercenary who served in the Roman army and later retired to northwest Germany, becoming a high-status member of the community who was honored with an alder-wood "throne" in his burial. But he also may have acquired the Roman belt through trade, inheritance or as a war trophy, the researchers wrote.

Either way, the man's skeleton and his grave goods suggest that northwest Germany had long-distance connections in Europe even after the fall of the Roman Empire, according to the statement.

Myburgh, D. A., da Silva, N. A., Romeyer-Dherbey, J. H., Grefen-Peters, S., Jöns, H., Peek, C., Nebel, A., & Krause-Kyora, B. (2026). Paleogenomics reveals leprosy at the late antique burial site of Fallward in northern Germany. iScience, 29(11), 117877. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117877

Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6281. Airport Luggage Tag Scam: How to Protect Your Checked Bags in 2026

Imagine walking up to customs after a long international flight and being told that a suitcase connected to your name has been flagged.

Then the officer points to the luggage tag and says, “Then why is your name on it?”

That is the nightmare behind a luggage scam travelers need to understand in 2026. It is called baggage tag switching, and it is exactly what it sounds like: the luggage tag from an innocent passenger’s checked suitcase is allegedly removed and placed onto another bag.

Baggage tag switching scams happen when the luggage tag from a traveler’s checked bag is allegedly removed and placed on another suitcase. To protect yourself, take a video of your suitcase before check-in, photograph the bag on the scale, take a close-up photo of the baggage tag, keep your baggage receipt, place a tracker inside your suitcase, and report any damaged, missing, delayed, or retagged bag before leaving the airport.

According to a W5 investigation, innocent passengers flying from Canada have been detained after their real luggage tags were allegedly moved onto suitcases containing illegal drugs. The investigation focused on flights from Canada and alleged cases connected to Toronto Pearson, but the larger lesson applies to travelers everywhere: once your checked bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting the system to protect your luggage, your tag, and your name.

We have traveled to more than 130 countries on all seven continents, and checked bags have always been part of travel. But the old habit of simply handing over your suitcase and hoping for the best needs an update.

In 2026, protecting your checked luggage is not just about stopping theft. It is about protecting the paper trail that connects you to your bag.

This is part of a bigger shift in how travelers need to think about airport safety, baggage scams, and common airport security mistakes before they fly.

Editor’s note: This article is based on our video about baggage tag switching, which has reached more than 86,000 views on our travel YouTube channel.

Before you check a bag, take two minutes to create proof that the bag is yours.

It also helps to run through a full pre-travel checklist before you leave for the airport so you are not rushing through check-in.

This may sound like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes at check-in. And those two minutes could matter if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

We covered this luggage tag scam in detail in the video below, including the simple two-minute routine we now recommend before checking a bag.

Baggage tag switching is when the tag printed for your checked luggage is removed from your actual suitcase and attached to another bag.

When you check luggage, the airline prints a baggage tag that usually includes your name, flight, destination, routing information, barcode, and bag number. That tag is the airport system’s way of connecting that suitcase to you.

The problem is that once your bag goes behind the counter, you cannot see what happens next.

In the alleged scheme reported by W5, corrupt baggage or ramp workers could remove a legitimate tag from a passenger’s suitcase and attach it to another suitcase heading to the same destination. If that second bag is intercepted, the paperwork points back to the innocent passenger.

That is what makes this scam so dangerous. You may have done everything right: checked your own suitcase, kept your boarding pass, and boarded your flight. But behind the scenes, one strip of paper may now connect your name to a bag you have never seen.

Most airport workers are honest. Let’s be clear about that. The vast majority are doing hard jobs under pressure, moving thousands of bags through complex systems every day. But a baggage system only needs a few bad actors to create a very serious problem.

This story has received attention because of Canadian cases, but this is not only a Canada problem.

The bigger issue is that every major airport has the same basic weak point: you hand over your suitcase, it enters a restricted area, and from that point on, you are relying on the system to protect the tag, the bag, and the records connected to your name.

That is true in Toronto. It is true in New York, London, Paris, Dubai, Bangkok, Mexico City, Sydney, and anywhere else checked luggage moves behind the scenes.

International travel also adds another layer of risk. If your name gets tied to a suspicious bag in another country, you may be dealing with a different legal system, different customs procedures, and possibly a language barrier.

The Government of Canada warns travelers that drug offences abroad can have serious consequences and that you should never carry anything across a border for someone else. The Canada Border Services Agency also specifically reminds travelers that trafficking cannabis or other drugs across the border is a criminal offence and warns people to beware of anyone asking them to carry something.

That is why documenting your own luggage matters. You are not being paranoid. You are creating a simple evidence trail.

Before your suitcase disappears behind the counter, take a clear video of it.

Do a full 360-degree view. Show the front, back, sides, wheels, handles, color, brand, straps, stickers, scratches, dents, or anything that makes your bag identifiable.

Yes, you may feel ridiculous filming your suitcase at the airport. Do it anyway. People film lattes. You can film the thing that might keep you out of a holding room.

This video creates a time-stamped record of what your suitcase looked like before it left your hands. If someone later claims a different bag is yours, you have proof of what your actual luggage looked like at check-in.

When your bag is placed on the airline scale, take a quick photo or video showing the weight.

This matters because weight is part of the paper trail. If your suitcase weighed 19 kilograms at check-in and another suitcase connected to your name weighs 32 kilograms, that difference may matter.

You are not trying to become a detective. You are simply creating a record that says this was your bag, this was the weight, this was the condition, and this was the tag attached to it.

That is the kind of simple documentation that can help if your bag is delayed, damaged, retagged, or questioned later.

Once the airline attaches the baggage tag to your suitcase, take a close-up photo or video of it before the bag goes onto the conveyor belt.

Make sure you can clearly see the barcode, destination airport, flight number, routing, and bag number. Also check that the airline has looped and attached the tag properly.

You are not being difficult. You are checking the one strip of paper connecting you to your luggage. That little tag is doing a lot of legal heavy lifting.

Air Canada’s own baggage information explains that self-service kiosks can print baggage tags, receipts, and boarding passes, and that travelers then attach the tags and proceed to bag drop. That means passengers are often handling or reviewing this paperwork themselves before the bag disappears into the system.

Never throw away the little baggage receipt sticker you receive at check-in.

Keep it somewhere safe. Don’t stuff it in a random pocket, lose it before boarding, or assume the airline app is enough. Put it with your passport or travel documents until your suitcase is back in your hands.

That receipt usually contains your bag number. If something goes wrong, that number becomes part of the evidence trail. That number can help airline staff or investigators compare what you checked, what arrived, and whether someone intercepted or retagged another bag.

This is one of the easiest travel habits to fix, and it costs nothing.

Before you close your checked bag, take one clear photo of the inside.

You do not need to photograph every sock like you are filing a museum inventory. Just take one clear photo of the contents: clothes, shoes, toiletries, chargers, jackets, and the usual chaos of travel.

This helps show what you actually packed. If a suitcase connected to your name contains items you have never seen, you have a record of what was inside your real bag before check-in.

This is especially useful on international trips, where proving what you packed may become more complicated once you are outside your home country.

It is also a good reminder to double-check what not to pack in checked luggage before you leave for the airport.

A luggage tracker will not stop someone from tampering with a baggage tag, but it can help show where your real suitcase went.

We use Apple AirTags, but there are also Tile trackers, Samsung SmartTags, and other luggage tracking options.

The important thing is this: put the tracker inside your suitcase. Do not hang it outside where it can easily be removed.

If authorities are asking about a suitcase connected to your name and your tracker shows your actual suitcase is somewhere else, that becomes another part of your evidence trail.

Trackers are also helpful if your bag arrives late, gets separated from its original tag, or ends up in the wrong baggage area. They are not perfect, but they give travelers one more layer of information when airline systems fail.

We use AirTags in our checked bags, but Samsung SmartTags and Tile trackers are also good options depending on your phone. The key is to keep the tracker inside the suitcase where it cannot easily be removed.

We also recommend pairing a luggage tracker with a few simple anti-theft travel accessories especially on longer international trips.

A plain black suitcase is basically the airport version of camouflage.

Make your luggage easier to identify with a bright strap, ribbon, sticker, or distinctive luggage tag. You want to be able to spot your bag quickly and prove what makes it different from hundreds of others.

But do not put too much personal information on the outside. Your name and phone number are enough.

You do not need your home address waving around the baggage hall like an invitation that says, “Please rob us while we’re in Italy.”

Keep luggage identifiable, but not overly revealing.

This rule has always mattered, but it matters even more now.

Never carry a package, gift, suitcase, envelope, or item for someone else. That means no favors for strangers, no “harmless” packages, and no quick airport errands for someone you barely know.

If you did not pack it, you do not carry it.

The CBSA specifically warns travelers to beware of people who ask them to carry anything and notes that consequences for drug trafficking can be serious in Canada and abroad.

That is the cleanest rule in travel: your bag, your responsibility.

If your checked bag arrives without the original tag, with a damaged tag, with a rush tag, or through a different baggage process than expected, do not just shrug and leave the airport.

Do not rely on a quick conversation at the counter. Conversations disappear the second you walk away. Written reports create a record.

This matters if your bag was mishandled, delayed, retagged, or separated from its original tag.

When your suitcase comes out at baggage claim, do not grab it on autopilot and leave.

Check that it is actually yours. Look at the tag, compare the bag number against your receipt, check your tracker, inspect the condition, and make sure the contents have not obviously been disturbed.

We have seen people accidentally walk away with someone else’s luggage. It happens more easily than people think, especially after long-haul flights when everyone is tired and half the carousel is filled with identical black suitcases.

Before you leave the airport or customs area, take one minute to confirm everything looks right.

Not necessarily. We have traveled for decades, and carry-on only is not always realistic. Sometimes you need to check a bag, especially on longer trips, family trips, cruises, cold-weather destinations, camera-heavy travel, or extended international travel.

For a smoother trip overall, our easy air travel tips can help before you even reach baggage claim.

For longer flights, our long-haul flight tips can also help make the journey easier before you even get to baggage claim.

The point is not to scare people out of checking luggage. The point is to update your habits.

The old way of checking luggage was simple: check the bag, keep the receipt somewhere, and hope for the best.

It sounds like a lot, but it takes less than two minutes — and those two minutes could make a huge difference if your name ever gets attached to a suitcase that is not yours.

If authorities ever question you about a suitcase that you do not recognize, stay calm.

Do not guess, don’t joke and do not become argumentative.

Ask for legal assistance and show the documentation you collected: your suitcase video, scale photo, baggage tag photo, receipt, tracker information, and photos of what you packed.

This article is not legal advice, but from a traveler’s perspective, the goal is simple: create proof before there is a problem.

If your name is ever attached to a bag you did not pack, your documentation may help show what your real suitcase looked like, what it weighed, what was inside it, and where it went.

Before every checked bag disappears behind the counter, take two minutes to create a simple record of your suitcase.

That’s it. Two minutes. No drama. No paranoia. Just smart travel.

Most airport workers are honest, and most checked bags arrive without a problem. But airport systems are massive, complicated, and not completely invisible-proof. Once your bag disappears behind the counter, you are trusting a chain of people, machines, tags, scans, and systems to keep your suitcase connected to your name.

So before your next flight, take two minutes to protect yourself. Film your bag. Photograph your tag. Keep your receipt. Use a tracker. And never carry anything for anyone else.

The goal is not to travel scared. The goal is to travel smarter.

Because when travelers get smarter, scams get riskier for the people trying to pull them off.

#6280. The Weber Genesis Costs Twice as Much as My Spirit Grill—and It’s Worth It

More space, faster heat, and better storage make this Weber worth the splurge.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Grilling has gotten me outside more than any other activity in the past two years, and—not to brag—I run a lot. Between hosting friends on any given three-day weekend, holiday parties, and weeknight dinners, I use my grill as much as possible. Weber’s Spirit grill was the gateway to this newfound personality trait. It evangelized me to propane grilling and outdoor cooking in general (my Recteq smoker deserves equal praise).

Growing up, my dad refused to cook on a gas grill, but I found charcoal time-consuming and messy as hell. My Spirit lights up fast, is easy to maintain, and was the perfect start to entrench me in the grilling lifestyle. However, nothing gold can stay, and I needed (ok, wanted) an upgrade.

Weber’s Genesis grills were the heir apparent. The range offers more storage, more power from each burner, and better overall build quality. On paper, it’s a clear upgrade from the brand’s Spirit line, but how does that translate in person? I found out it’s a well-worth-it upgrade that elevates my grilling experience.

I love Weber, but I admit the names can be a bit complicated. At least the naming system is consistent across the brand, as I ran into the same thing when shopping Spirit grills. The letters and numbers describe the materials used, the number of burners, and each grill's features. Here’s a quick and easy breakdown:

My Spirit grill was an E-210, and my Genesis is an E-330. The obvious difference is the extra burner on the Genesis, but both are base models in their respective lineups, making them easier to compare.

Improved build quality is a tricky thing to discern from a product listing. It’s subjective, since people define quality differently, but in my opinion, the Genesis is indeed improved. It feels much more substantial than the Spirit in hand, with sturdy metal hardware, and I immediately noticed the difference when I separated the parts and hardware for the Genesis. There’s a lot less plastic, and everything feels secure.

The Genesis also has a cleaner design, which makes storage more efficient. An extra side cabinet stores grates and accessories, and the propane cabinet has room for even more. Four locking caster wheels prop the grill and propane tank up off the ground. On the Spirit, the propane tank sits on the ground, making it hard to move.

Two side tables provide plenty of prep space and don’t fold down as they do on the Spirit. They can be swapped out for Weber Works accessories, letting me reconfigure the grill to my cooking needs.

Grills are aesthetically pleasing to me as is, but even more so when it comes to Weber’s Stealth Edition grills. They feature an all-black design with a matte black lid, black trim, side tables, handles, knobs, wheels, and a separate sear burner controlled by a metallic red knob. The Stealth Edition costs about $200 extra, so it's up to you whether it’s worth it.

Going from two burners to three burners inevitably adds cooking space, but I didn’t expect to love it this much. I went from 450 square inches of primary cooking space (not including the top rack) on the Spirit to 513 square inches on the Genesis. Only 73 inches more, but it feels so much bigger in action, and I no longer need to cook in batches for large groups.

The extra burner also means it heats up much faster than my old grill. When searing Force of Nature and Snake River Farms NY strip and ribeyes, I got the grill up to 500 degrees Fahrenheit in about two and a half minutes. All that extra firepower also makes the warming rack a bona fide cooking space on its own. I grilled burgers on the primary space while fully cooking hot dogs on the warming rack over Labor Day weekend.

The Genesis grates can also be flipped and reconfigured with Weber Crafted accessories. This lets you expand cooking methods and upgrade grates and cookware later, so you don’t get bored with your setup.

I’ll always have a place in my heart for my Spirit grill. It’s small, efficient, and saw me through many block parties and gatherings, but it was time for a change. The Weber Genesis E-330 is the perfect mid-range upgrade I was looking for—more space, more firepower, and more storage. All of these features have improved my grilling experience and made it markedly more enjoyable. I realize the price difference is nothing to scoff at; $500 isn’t chump change, but it’s worth the splurge if you know you want to grill often

#6279. Where to Find the Fastest Delivery for the iPhone Duo

Apple picking is an annual autumn rite, but when it comes to shopping Apple’s first folding phone, retailers have mostly bare branches.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Apple sure underestimated how many people would scramble for an iPhone Duo. Tsunamis of anticipation over the first folding iPhone had built up over years, long before Apple made it official and announced it on October 16, 2026, but how many people would rush to buy a smartphone that starts at $1,999?

It took hardly a day to find out. Perhaps it had something to do with us declaring it the best folding phone yet. During the week prior to the iPhone Duo’s October 23 launch day, when those with a taste for Apple’s latest phone could preorder it on Apple.com, the ship date list stretched into January as people gobbled up the early batch of available units. And on launch day itself, local news everywhere ran story after story about long lines outside Apple stores, with many going home empty-handed before closing time as the Duo quickly sold out.

You can walk into an Apple store and try your luck, although I wouldn’t count on walking out with one in hand. Many Apple stores I’ve checked in big cities have none available for pickup. You can still order one online at Apple, as long as you’re fine with waiting until January 25 to get yours.

You can find the iPhone Duo at Best Buy for Verizon and AT&T. Switching up the color between Night Sky (black) and Star White, or the storage capacity (256GB, 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB), or the carrier, does not change the December 22 shipping or pickup date.

Heading to your local cellular carrier’s retail store may be your best bet for landing an iPhone Duo before Christmas, but like with the Apple Store, I wouldn’t count on it. Verizon casts a wide net for its estimated ship date: December 12–30. Those ordered from T-Mobile won’t make the Christmas cut. As of today, the backordered phone shows a ship date of December 31-January 6. And AT&T may have the longest ship time of all, as its ordering pages offer shipping “As soon as January 6,” which hints that the 6th is the earliest you may expect your AT&T-linked iPhone Duo, but that it may come later.

Interestingly, no matter how I configured each one in any color and storage combination, the estimated ship dates at all three carriers stayed the same. In past years at Apple launches, devices with higher capacities (and correspondingly higher price tags) tended to be available sooner. Not so this time with the iPhone Duo. Just remember that if you buy a phone from one network, it’s not guaranteed to work on another. If you want an unlocked iPhone Duo that’ll work on any cellular network, you’ll have to order it from Apple and practice patience until it ships in early 2027.

Walmart has listed product pages for the iPhone Duo since Apple announced it, but I’ve yet to see anybody actually able to order one there. I’ve kept a near-daily eye on the Walmart page, though, and every combination of color, carrier, and storage option has been out of stock and unavailable to backorder since the iPhone Duo’s debut.

If you’re on the fence, don’t expect the waitlist to shorten while you wring your hands. Occasionally, ship dates for hot, newly released devices move up as retailers receive new batches, but I’ve been keeping a close eye on the iPhone Duo for the past three weeks and haven’t seen that happen at any retailer, including Apple itself. The ship dates we’ve provided here are current as of today. They can only get longer from here.

Researchers used CT scans to crack a 400-year-old code and open a mysterious padlock that washed up in Wales with the Ann Francis treasure hoard.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Elizabethan padlock has been opened for the first time in more than 400 years after researchers used X-ray imaging techniques to crack its four-letter combination.

The brass lock was part of the Ann Francis treasure hoard, named after the British merchant ship that wrecked during a storm off the coast of Wales in 1583. Researchers believe the lock once secured a chest aboard the ship, before becoming separated from whatever riches it was protecting.

Some of the Ann Francis' cargo was recovered at the time of the wreck, while the rest was claimed by the sea. In recent decades, dredging and storms on Margam beach in South Wales have exposed some of the ship's lost treasure.

Between 1996 and 2017, metal detectorist Peter Hughes found the lock and much of the hoard, which included gold and silver coins. The lock was subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru — National Museum Wales, which worked with researchers at Cardiff University in Wales to decipher its combination.

To study the lock's internal mechanisms, the team used micro-CT scans, which make thousands of X-rays that can then be configured into a 3D digital image. By matching internal notches to external letters in the digital 3D image, the researchers were able to decipher the correct four-letter code — "ANCE" — and open the lock.

"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," David Williams, a research associate at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University, said in a statement. "It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!"

The Ann Francis was owned by Francis Shaxton, a merchant and notorious smuggler. Francis claimed the ship was sailing along the eastern English coast from King’s Lynn to Hartlepool, when it was actually traveling in the opposite direction, heading to Spain to deliver a cargo of wheat. Spain was dependent on grain shipments at the time and paid for such shipments in gold and silver from colonial conquests in Central and South America, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The ship was traveling back from Spain to England when, on the evening of Dec. 28, 1583, it was caught in a violent storm. After heading off course, the ship ended its journey in ruin off Margam beach.

A parish register noted the loss of 14 sailors during the same month as the wreckage, which could have been The Ann Francis's crew, according to Amgueddfa Cymru. The deaths were blamed on the nefarious work of a supposed witch.

Locals were quick to loot the Ann Francis wreck before a legal dispute ensued over who had the right to its goods. One Welsh lord claiming the wreck made an inventory list of items he impounded, which included cannons, guns, a piece of mast, Spanish silver and three chests with their locks broken. The newly cracked lock could have originally secured one of these chests, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Centuries after the ship was wrecked, Hughes found the lock near a previously undiscovered stash of Spanish silver coins and coin weights while metal detecting on the beach.

"When I found the lock I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition," Hughes said. "When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief."

Hughes said he attempted to open the lock himself over many years but could never find the right combination. After Amgueddfa Cymru acquired the lock, staff were concerned that they could hear grit moving around inside the dials, and with more than 1,000 possible combinations, they didn't want to cause any damage.

The micro-CT scans offered a nondestructive view inside the lock, and an opportunity to finally identify the correct four-letter combination.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve," Alastair Willis, the senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said in the statement. "Of course, now we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."
